feat(validate): catch invented tenure, certifications and education (#1024)

* test(validate): measure the credential extractors before they earn a severity

Years of experience, certifications and education are three invention classes
no shipped check can see: MetricKind is {Percent, Multiplier, LargeInteger} and
a bare one- or two-digit number is deliberately not policed, so "8+ years of
experience" on a source showing four passes every check we have.

The extractors land first, wired to NOTHING and gated behind cfg(test). This
module has already shipped one false Critical on a truthful résumé, and one here
is expensive: a Critical blanks keywordCoverage and suppresses every alignment
finding on a document that is fine. So the measurement comes before the
severity, not after it.

Measured over 13 known-truthful documents (both clean fixtures, both
paraphrased, both projects tiers, the grounded letter, both eval-corpus résumés,
plus new cross-language and certification-bearing probes):

  years          0 false positives   (8 documents state a tenure that was read
                                      and cleared, so the zero is not vacuous)
  certifications 0 false positives   (2 documents carry 5 extracted claims,
                                      including a German rendering of an English
                                      source's AWS and CKA certifications)
  education by VALUE      1 false positive
  education by ABSENCE    0 false positives

The education false positive is the one the design predicted: city names
translate exactly as degree titles do, so a correct German "Technische
Universität München" for an English source's "Technical University of Munich"
shares no token with it and reads as an invention.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* feat(validate): catch invented tenure, certifications and education

Three invention classes the metric family cannot see, wired in with the tiers
the calibration commit measured rather than the tiers their names suggest.

factual.inflated_experience (Critical). Compares the NUMBER in "8+ years of
experience" against what the source states in words and against the span its
own employment dates cover, plus one year of slack for the months a year column
does not carry. Only an OVERSTATEMENT fires: rounding down is not a fabrication,
so the rule is "must not exceed", never "must appear". Comparing numbers is what
makes this survive a German résumé generated from an English source, which is
the path #1004 shipped.

factual.unsourced_certification (Critical). A curated issuer list plus a curated
acronym list, never "looks capitalised". A certification word with no issuer
near it is not a credential, so "certified the release each Thursday" reports
nothing. CSM and CPA are left out of the acronym list by name: both are real
certifications and neither is unambiguous.

factual.unsourced_institution (Warning, absence only). A2c was specified as a
value comparison on the institution name. Measured, it produced a false finding
on truthful cross-language output: "Technische Universität München" is the
correct German rendering of an English source's "Technical University of
Munich" and shares no token with it. City names translate exactly as degree
titles do. What ships instead is the translation-safe residue — the generated
document names a place of study while the source names none at all — and it
stays advisory even there. The rejected comparison is still executed by
institution_value_comparison_fires_on_a_correctly_translated_institution, so
the rejection keeps being true rather than being a comment.

The tenure check reads the clock once, to close an open-ended "2019 - Present",
and validates it: a clock reading earlier than a year the documents name is
discarded along with the span evidence instead of shrinking the allowance into
an accusation.

Both Criticals join report::FABRICATION_CODES because a Critical that is not
listed there keeps its run in needsReview forever, and neither has a section the
repair loop could regenerate - SectionKey has no Certifications variant.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(validate): stop the credential checks firing on truthful résumés

Six defects, every one reproduced by execution before it was fixed and pinned
by a test with a mutation check behind it. The calibration corpus grows from 13
truthful documents to 21: the zero it reported was real for the corpus and
uninformative about the population, because two documents were graded against
themselves and nine of the rest shared two source fixtures. Each register added
here produced one of the false Criticals below.

Certifications, prose. The issuer pass accepted any issuer token within 60
characters of any certification word, and "certified" is a past-tense verb at
least as often as an adjective: four of four realistic bullets fired. The
CLAIMS side now requires the issuer and the certification word to be adjacent
tokens; the SOURCE side keeps the wide window, so Source is still a superset of
Claims and the leniency now falls on the sparing side.

Certifications, two namespaces. The acronym pass emitted `cka` and the issuer
pass emitted `kubernetes`, and the comparison is on keys — so a source holding
`Certified Kubernetes Administrator` did not support a generated `CKA`, nor the
reverse. Acronyms now carry the key their expansion resolves to, plus the
expansion itself for the ones whose long form names no issuer (`CISSP`, `PMP`).
The old negative test passed only because its fixture wrote both forms on one
line; each fixture now names exactly one.

Tenure, three ways the span was shrunk into an accusation. `is_open_ended` does
not know `Actualidad`, `Aujourd'hui` or `Today`, and the span then closed at the
role's own START year; `factual::entries` cannot see a block headed `EARLIER
ROLES`, so a 2010 role vanished; and neither can see an `EXPERIENCIA` heading at
all. All three are the same defect — the sparing half of the comparison reads
raw text and the accusing half read a parse. Both ends are now read off text:
the earliest year anywhere in the source, to today when a structural scan finds
a span whose separator is not followed by another year. That test is
language-independent, so it also covers the next spelling of "present" nobody
has listed.

Tenure, en/de number words. `quinze ans`, `quince años`, `quindici anni`,
`vijftien jaar` all extracted to nothing, so a French source stating its tenure
in words could not spare a faithful restatement of it in digits. The table now
covers every language the pipeline writes, and a quantifier it still cannot read
("several years") silences the check rather than being read as zero. This is the
"translation-safe by construction" claim failing where it mattered: the
comparison is on a number, but the extraction of the sparing evidence was not.

Tenure, the summary bypass. Admitting every `<number> <year-word>` in a summary
made "replaced a 30 year old mainframe" a tenure claim. Dropped; a real claim
carries an experience word anyway. Measured cost: `de_generated_clean` still
extracts its "Acht Jahre Erfahrung", `en_generated_clean`'s "Eight years of
backend work" no longer extracts at all.

Education. The absence guard was decided by lexicon coverage rather than by the
document — `IIT Delhi` carries no marker word, so a truthful entry under a
`QUALIFICATIONS` heading looked like an invented one. A degree token is now the
third layer of the guard.

Also corrected: `factual.inflated_experience` DOES route to SectionKey::Summary,
so a false positive would have spent repair calls rewriting a correct summary —
the FABRICATION_CODES comment said the opposite. `factual.unsourced_institution`
leaves that list, because a Warning listed there parks its run in needsReview
and "advisory" that blocks a run is not advisory. The clock's determinism
caveat is now stated where it is read.

Measured after the fixes: 0 false positives across 21 truthful documents for
both Criticals and for the shipped education Warning, with recall unchanged on
all three planted inventions.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(validate): make the tenure check a warning, and stop it being an off switch

The calibration now asserts on the EXTRACTED column, not only the flagged one.
That gap is why both of this round's over-corrections shipped past a green
harness: a check that has been switched off and a check that has been fixed
both report zero false positives. The set of fixtures whose extraction is
non-empty is pinned as a hand-written membership list — a set compared against
itself cannot notice a deletion, which is the exact failure being guarded.

The unreadable-tenure guard was an off switch. It matched any letter-word
before any year-word anywhere in the source, so one bullet reading "Cut cloud
spend by 1.2M USD per year" silenced factual.inflated_experience for the whole
document; "year over year growth", "the fiscal year close" and "last year" did
the same. It is now scoped by the admission rule the claims side uses, so
"several years of experience" still silences and an impact figure does not.

Removing the summary bypass cost six of twenty-one fixtures their extraction,
not the one previously reported — including the two sentences this repo's own
truthful fixtures write verbatim ("Eight years of backend work, most of it on
payment systems", "Backend engineer with 8 years building distributed
services"). Removing it was right; removing it without widening what the gate
admits was not. The summary admission is back and shape-aware: the span must
open a clause, preceded by nothing or by a lead-in word, and be followed by a
preposition or participle. The three legacy-system sentences fail both halves
independently.

Attributive vendor terms are no longer credentials. "Docker Certified images",
"Red Hat certified build images", "VMware certified storage arrays" and
"Certified Scrum team" are grammatically identical to a real credential, and
adjacency alone could not tell them apart — seven of seven fired. A
certification names a ROLE its holder is certified to fill, so one must appear
within a bounded window after it.

Decades were covered by neither the number table nor the guard, and both a
comment and a test doc claimed otherwise. "over a decade of experience" now
reads as an unmeasurable tenure rather than an absent one; it is not mapped to
ten, because "over a decade" is anywhere from ten to nineteen and picking a
number invents evidence on the sparing side.

A numeric month after an opener no longer closes a span. "Seit 03/2016" wants a
year within one word of the opener to satisfy is_open_ended, so the current role
read as closed at its own start year.

Two MEDIUMs: one certification named in both its forms is one finding, not two;
and the "Source is a superset of Claims" claim is now stated with the bound it
actually holds under.

## The severity call

factual.inflated_experience ships as a WARNING. The criterion permitted a
Critical — zero false positives across 25 truthful documents while reading the
tenure sentences this repo's fixtures write verbatim — and the argument against
is the shape of the input rather than the number. Two review rounds found five
distinct registers that each produced a false Critical, and the corpus was green
before every one of them was named; the claims side reads unbounded prose in
seven languages discriminated by three hand-curated word lists. The cost is
asymmetric too: this code routes to SectionKey::Summary, so a false one would
spend provider calls rewriting a correct summary and could pressure the model
into understating a tenure the candidate really has. A Warning cannot —
criticals_by_section never sees it, and it leaves FABRICATION_CODES with the
other Warning.

factual.unsourced_certification stays Critical: its trigger is three bounded
vocabularies intersecting, not prose.

credentials.rs reached 1397 of R8's 1400-line hard cap, so the three families
move into credentials/{tenure,certifications,education}.rs behind a flat
re-export. The parent keeps the dispatcher and the one helper both certification
and education passes share.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(validate): split the certification code by evidence, and stop the tenure shape reading systems

Round four. The severity work is the substance: `factual.unsourced_certification`
covered two arms resting on different evidence, and only one of them earned a
Critical.

The ACRONYM arm matches an uppercase, word-bounded token from a curated
23-entry list. It reads no prose, each token means one thing on a résumé in any
language, and three review rounds produced no false positive from it. It stays
Critical.

The ISSUER arm reads unbounded natural language in seven languages,
discriminating with adjacency plus three curated vocabularies. It shipped "4 of
4 fixed, measured" and broke on the next pass; it shipped "7 of 7 fixed,
measured" and broke on the next pass again. That is the evidence class the
tenure check already ships as a Warning, with the same cadence, so it becomes
factual.unsourced_credential at Warning severity. Two codes rather than one,
because `issue` reads severity from the code table — which is what makes the
Critical unreachable from the prose path.

The clause-shape rule read sentences about SYSTEMS as claims about people,
fifteen times out of fifteen: "Rebuilt a platform with 15 years of accumulated
technical debt", "Joined a team with 12 years of shipping history", and the same
shape in six more languages built from these very lead-in and follower lists.
The discriminator was measured and it is in the SUBJECT position — false ones
end in platform, team, codebase, stack, ledger, service, mainframe; truthful
ones in engineer, developer, designer, Ingenieurin, or open the line. So the
subject must name a person or be absent. Two tokens of it are read, because a
job title is routinely two words and the head noun comes last in some languages
and first in others. The follower list is deliberately not where this is fixed:
of, in, on and at follow any counted noun phrase whatever.

The role-noun rule did not fix the vendor terms. `engineer` matched as a
substring of `engineers` anywhere within 48 characters, so every case from the
round before revived with one extra word on the end. The window is now two
TOKENS, which is where a credential actually names its role.

A bare acronym under a Certifications heading was invisible: `split_sections`
promotes a lone `CISSP` to a heading, so it lived in `Section::heading` and no
line scan saw it. Sixteen of the twenty-three curated acronyms are four
characters or more and were reachable that way — a hole in the one arm whose
evidence justifies a Critical. Headings are scanned now.

Also: a certification named in both its forms deduplicates to the ACRONYM
finding rather than to whichever came first, so document order cannot decide a
severity; role nouns gain designer, programmer, specialty, fundamentals and
belt; and two docs are corrected — the stale one on `years_claims` that still
claimed the context word was the only admission rule, and the superset claim,
which is true of the claims-side predicate rather than of every reading.

Measured after the change: 0 false positives across 25 truthful documents for
every arm, all 14 tenure-stating documents still read, recall held on all four
planted inventions, and 14 of 14 mutation checks re-verified by execution. One
of those was found unguarded during the re-verification — deleting the adjacency
rule left the suite green, because the tightened role-noun window rejected the
old fixtures on its own — and now has a case that binds it.

* fix(validate): stop derivational nouns from being misread as a role noun

names_a_role matched ROLE_NOUNS as an unanchored substring, so
architecture/engineering/expertise (none of which name a person) satisfied
it via architect/engineer/expert, letting a truthful summary line about a
platform or a practice fire factual.inflated_experience, and loosening
certifications::names_a_certified_role the same way. Replace the bare

* fix(pipeline): resolve a fabrication removal by its anchored line, not a recurring bare token

entry_resolved checked only entry.evidence for a "remove" verdict, and
evidence is routinely a bare token (a certification acronym, a bare year, a
bare figure) that can legitimately recur on a DIFFERENT line the user never
touched - a project bullet naming the same acronym, say. Searching for it
anywhere in the document asks "does this substring still exist", not "is
the flagged bullet gone", and stranded a genuinely-applied Remove in
needsReview forever. Read the entry's own line anchor first (the exact span
containing_line already computed for this purpose) and fall back to
evidence only when no line was recorded.

The renderer half of the same bug (isFabricationResolved/evidencePresent in
lib/generate/fabrications.ts) is unfixed here - reported to frontend-author.

* fix(validate): stop two distinct certifications from one issuer collapsing into one finding

unsupported_certs deduped every claim on keys[0], the ISSUER key - but CKA
and CKS (and CCNA/CCNP) both key to the same issuer (kubernetes, cisco)
while naming two DIFFERENT certifications. A document inventing both
reported only the first; the second silently dropped off the review, a
recall loss on the sole Critical arm. Dedup the acronym arm on its own
spelling instead (unique per credential), and have each accepted acronym
claim its issuer so a matching issuer-phrase claim for the SAME credential
still merges into it - preserving "one credential written both ways is one
finding" while fixing the two-distinct-inventions case.

Also hoists line.to_lowercase() out of the 23-iteration acronym loop in
cert_claims_on_line (23 allocations per source line down to 1); no behavior
change.

* fix(validate): a scrum master credential no longer satisfies the education gate

names_a_degree read "master" out of "Certified Scrum Master" just as
readily as out of "Master of Science" (contains_phrase is word-bounded,
not context-aware), so a source naming ONLY that credential - no real
education section, no institution word - satisfied source_has_education
and silenced unsourced_institution for a document that invented a school
whole. Exclude the exact "scrum master(s)" phrase rather than dropping the
token outright, so a bare "Master, IIT Delhi" line still counts.

Also adds the dedup unsupported_institutions was missing (its two sibling
arms, tenure and certifications, already dedup on their own key) - the
same invented school named twice in an Education section no longer reports
as two identical Warnings.

* fix(validate): deduplicate the spelled-number alternation vocabulary

YEARS_RE built its word list with sort_by_key(Reverse(len)) then dedup(),
but Vec::dedup only removes CONSECUTIVE equal elements and sorting by
LENGTH groups equal lengths, not equal strings - so cross-language repeats
in SPELLED_NUMBERS (quatorze: French and Portuguese; tres: Spanish and
Portuguese) survived the dedup call the comment above it claimed removed
them. Not a correctness bug - both copies map to the same value, so the
regex still matches identically - but the doc comment asserted a property
the code did not provide. Extract the word list into its own function,
sort-and-dedup by VALUE first, then re-sort by length for the alternation's
longest-first requirement.

feat(match): report hard constraints beside the score instead of blending them into it (#1023)

* feat(match): report hard constraints beside the score instead of blending them into it

Track E1 of the architecture audit.

`combined = f(semantic, ats)` measures how much of a posting's vocabulary the
résumé carries. It is a good relevance number and it structurally cannot answer
"could I actually take this job?", so a candidate who fails a non-negotiable
still scores well on keyword overlap. The fix is not to fold a penalty into the
number — it is to answer the second question separately.

`match_resume` now returns a `constraints.checks` field beside the score. Three
rules hold it up:

* it never touches the score. The verdict is computed in the L3 command AFTER
  the kernel returns, so it is not an input to `score_one` and never enters the
  `match_scores` cache — whose key is composed of SCORING inputs only, and would
  therefore have served a stale verdict for a whole TTL the moment the user
  edited their preferences. Out here, a cache HIT still gets a fresh verdict,
  and the Autopilot and extension entry points that share the kernel are
  byte-identical;
* it never hides a job. Nothing filters, sorts or gates on it. A wrong knock-out
  tells the user not to bother applying, which costs far more than a wrong
  percentage;
* absence of evidence is never evidence. `ConstraintStatus` has FOUR values, and
  the two "we don't know" ones are distinct from both a pass and a fail:
  `unknown` (the candidate stated a preference, the posting says nothing, or
  what they stated is not comparable) and `noPreference` (the candidate has
  expressed nothing at all — differently actionable, since the user can fix that
  one). A `notMet` requires positive evidence on BOTH sides, and each check
  carries each side's own words so that is a checkable property of the payload
  rather than a promise. It is enforced inside the one constructor every check
  goes through, not as a post-pass a later constraint could skip.

ONE constraint ships, because one is what the app has honest candidate-side data
for. `location`: the user's stored job-search location (and its geocode-picked
country code) against the posting's location text and its board remote flag.
Both sides are real, persisted, user-entered data.

The audit's other three are refused, and the module says so in full:

* work authorization, ranked first, has NO candidate-side field anywhere — not
  on the contact profile, not in job preferences. The tempting proxy, the
  candidate's own address, is exactly the false accusation this repo already has
  a live incident from: living in one country is not evidence of lacking
  authorization in another;
* employment type has no persisted preference. `AutopilotTarget::work_type` is a
  per-autopilot SEARCH filter, and a work arrangement rather than an employment
  type;
* salary floor: `salary_expectation` is free text ("80k DOE") documented as an
  application ANSWER, not a stated floor, with no currency and no period, and
  the posting side is a structured range on one board. Comparing them needs a
  money parser plus an FX assumption — two invented facts per verdict.

The comparison itself reuses the scrape-time location matcher rather than
forking one. `location_filter` grows a three-valued `location_verdict`, and the
existing binary `location_mismatch` is redefined as exactly its `Mismatch`
projection — same behaviour, one home for the remote-marker list, the diaeresis
folding and the curated exonym table. `languages_align` does not apply: nothing
here reads the résumé or the JD body, stems a token or extracts a keyword.

Mutation-checked, ten ways. Two survived the first round and both were real
holes, now closed: the two-sided-evidence guard was a post-pass its test called
directly, so deleting it from `evaluate` stayed green — it is a constructor now;
and deleting the one line that wires the pass into the command left the whole
suite green, because a `#[tauri::command]` cannot be called from a test in this
crate, so a compile-time source scan pins it. The other eight — rendering
unknown as a pass, dropping the no-preference branch, deleting either remote
feature, dropping the posting-side evidence, making the scrape filter drop on
undecided, folding the verdict into `combined`, removing the evidence byte cap —
each fail by name.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(match): stop the location constraint publishing a knock-out it cannot justify

Review was right on both counts, and the shipped verdict was the defect.

The first cut published `notMet` for location. Two independent facts say it
must not:

* the candidate side is a search-personalization setting, not a mobility
  statement. `job_preferences.location` is written by one free-text "Preferred
  Location" input whose own description says it "personalizes search results and
  recommendations". `JobsPage` seeds its scrape form from it ONE WAY and never
  writes back, so a user who deliberately searches Austin while Settings still
  says Berlin leaves no trace. `PostingsCache` keeps postings from every past
  search and retains no per-posting `LocationSpec`, so this pass cannot even
  recover which search a posting came from — the honest sentence would have been
  "a setting you last touched months ago says Berlin", against every cached row;
* a failed substring match is absence of evidence, not evidence of conflict.
  `Mismatch` fires on `Germany`/`Berlin` (granularity), `Vienna`/`Wien` and
  `NYC`/`New York` (exonym and abbreviation outside the curated table),
  `Berlin`/`EMEA` and `Berlin`/`Multiple locations` (not place names), and
  `Berlin`/`Telecommute` (a remote synonym the marker list lacks). It would also
  fire across most of the primary aggregator: Adzuna never writes
  `extra.remote` — only the three remote-only boards do — so remote detection
  there rests entirely on location text Adzuna's `display_name` never carries.

The module's own rule 3 convicted it: two non-empty strings satisfied the
constructor's floor while not being evidence of a CONTRADICTION.

So `Mismatch` now maps to `Unknown`, and the location check emits `Met` /
`Unknown` / `NoPreference` only. `Met` survives on positive evidence in both
directions and never accuses. The three-valued matcher still earns its keep —
without it `Met` could not be told apart from "the posting states no location".

The severity distinction is the lesson, and it is recorded in the module: the
identical predicate is safe as a scrape-time post-filter, judging a posting
against a location the user typed seconds earlier and costing one row in one
search, and unsafe as a published verdict against every cached posting keyed off
a settings field. Reuse the matcher; re-derive the epistemics.

Net result for Track E1: NO shipped constraint can emit a knock-out.
`ConstraintStatus::NotMet` stays as the contract slot a future constraint with
real two-sided evidence will use, and a test pins that it is unreachable rather
than merely unused.

Also fixed:

* the wiring pin was blind to a present-but-dead call. It now matches the call
  as a WHOLE LINE, which rejects both `let _ = constraints::attach(…)` and a
  commented-out call, and leans on the compiler for the rest: the line carries
  no trailing semicolon, and a `Value`-typed expression statement that is not
  the tail does not compile. The first version embedded a closing brace in a
  string literal, which silently truncated the region the egress inventory's
  naive brace counter strips from this file — caught by that guard, fixed here
  rather than added to its exception list;
* the constructor was not the structural guarantee its doc claimed. Rust field
  privacy is module-scoped, so a struct literal compiled anywhere inside
  `mod constraints` — exactly where the next constraint gets written. The type
  is sealed in its own `mod check` now, and the bypass is a compile error;
* `isKnockOut(check)` ships beside `ConstraintStatus` before any UI reads it:
  `status !== 'met'` silently turns both unknowable states into an accusation;
* `country_code` was inert on both ends — no renderer writes it, and the matcher
  draws needles from city/region text only. Dropped rather than left as a claim
  the code does not honour.

Tests: the review's pairs are asserted individually and as a corpus, and the old
`knock_outs == 4` — which could only confirm the code agreed with itself, its
corpus holding only pairings it already agreed with — is replaced by the full
status distribution over 140 cells (40 noPreference, 58 met, 42 unknown, 0
notMet), hand-derived so it cannot pass by collapsing to one answer.

Mutation-checked 14 ways, all caught, including the two the review named:
`let _ = constraints::attach(…)` is red, and the struct-literal bypass no longer
compiles. Re-publishing `notMet` for a failed place-name match is red. The TS
predicate mutated to `status !== 'met'` fails 3 tests.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(match): require a whole-token place match before claiming a location fits

The four-state contract's one confident state was still loose. `met` is a
positive claim rendered to the user — "this posting matches where you're
looking" — and it rested on the scrape filter's substring, any-token reading, so
a `San Francisco` preference agreed with a `San Diego` posting on the shared
`san`. Erring toward agreement rather than accusation makes that cheap, not
correct. A contract whose only confident state is loose has moved the
imprecision, not removed it.

The strictness lives in the epistemics layer, not in the shared matcher: the
scrape filter's conservatism is right where it is, because there the expensive
mistake is discarding a job.

So the matcher now reports WHAT it found and the constraint pass decides what is
claimable. `LocationVerdict::Match` splits three ways:

* `Remote` — the board flagged it or its location text carries a marker, so no
  place comparison applies;
* `PlaceMatch` — every token the user actually typed appears as a WHOLE token of
  the posting's location;
* `PlaceOverlap` — something matched, but only as a substring or on part of a
  multi-token request.

`location_mismatch` is still exactly the `Mismatch` projection, so the scrape
filter is byte-for-byte unchanged: `PlaceOverlap` keeps, as it always did. The
constraint pass maps `Remote | PlaceMatch` to `met` and everything else,
`PlaceOverlap` included, to `unknown`.

Exonyms are expanded PER TOKEN in the strict matcher rather than over the whole
needle list. Expansion adds a word the user never wrote — a "Munich" request
gains "münchen" — so requiring every needle in the expanded list to match would
fail the exact pair the curated table exists to bridge.

The cost is deliberate and one-directional: a request MORE specific than the
posting ("Berlin, Germany" against a bare "Berlin") now reads `unknown` rather
than `met`. That loses a true positive and never states a false one, and
`unknown` claims nothing.

Tests: a dedicated overlap case (San Diego, Santa Monica, Newark, and the
more-specific request) with a same-preference control that still reads `met`, so
this is a strictness rule and not a blanket refusal to match a two-token place.
The 140-cell distribution grows to 176 (11 places × 8 preferences × 2 flags) to
carry the San Francisco / San Diego pairing, and its hand-derived counts — 44
noPreference, 75 met, 57 unknown, 0 notMet — are what fail if the strict rule is
relaxed: that one cell moves from unknown to met.

Mutation-checked 19 ways, all caught. New this round: publishing `met` for an
overlap, grading every hit as a whole-token match, requiring only SOME requested
token instead of every one, dropping the per-token exonym expansion, degrading
the whole-token test to a substring test, and making the scrape filter drop on
an overlap.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(match): bound the met claim to the setting it reads, and pin what it rests on

Five review findings. The first is the one that mattered: the epistemics were
re-derived in ONE direction only.

Every fact used to kill `notMet` is direction-neutral — `job_preferences.location`
is a search-personalization setting, `JobsPage` seeds from it one-way, and
`PostingsCache` keeps postings from every past search with no record of which
`LocationSpec` produced them. So the mirror case was equally false: the same
stale `Berlin` setting, against `Berlin` rows left over from an earlier search,
reported `met` — and if that rendered as "this posting matches where you're
looking" it was wrong for the same reason, from the same field.

Deleting `met` is not the answer; it would leave a contract with no positive
state and make the pass vacuous. The asymmetry is real and it is in what each
status ASSERTS:

* `notMet` asserted a CONFLICT — that the posting is somewhere the candidate will
  not go. Nothing establishes that relation, and no phrasing repairs it, because
  the fact was never in hand;
* `met` asserts a MATCH between two strings held in full. The relation — every
  token of the stored preference present in the posting's location — is
  established deterministically and stays true whichever search produced the row.

So `met` is repaired by bounding what it is a claim ABOUT. It says "your stored
Preferred Location matches this posting", never "matches where you're looking".
Fixed where the meaning is defined, since there is no renderer yet to correct
later: the check's wire id is now `preferredLocation` rather than `location` —
the id is what a renderer keys i18n off, so it is what stops the stronger
sentence being written by accident, and it leaves `location` free for a real
mobility constraint if candidate-side data ever exists. Also stated on the
variant, the module doc, and the three shared TS docs a UI author reads.

Also fixed:

* `met` for the shipped UI defaults silently depended on `MIN_TOKEN_LEN`. "San
  Francisco, CA", "New York, NY" and "London, UK" all read as matches ONLY
  because 3 drops the two-letter qualifier, while that constant's doc justified
  3 purely as scrape-filter noise control. Lowering it to 2 for a scrape-side
  reason flipped all three to `unknown` with nothing failing. Now pinned by
  test, and the constant records that it has a second consumer with a different
  risk posture;
* the verdict and the evidence were computed from different bytes — the
  unclamped location was compared, the clamped one reported — so a >200-byte
  location could match on a token outside its own evidence. Both sides are
  clamped once, before the comparison. The test is a replay: re-running the
  evaluation on exactly what the check REPORTS must reproduce what it decided;
* `checks_for_job` took the `PostingsCache` lock and re-scanned for a job id
  `job_text_for` had just scanned for. Since the verdict is deliberately
  recomputed on a `match_scores` cache HIT, that duplicate ran on every
  Jobs-page call — the path where the score costs nothing. The posting is
  resolved once and handed over; the pure half is split out so the hand-off is
  testable;
* `PlaceOverlap` named two situations of opposite evidential strength: a
  coincidental substring ("San Francisco"/"San Diego" on `san`) and a genuine
  whole-token hit with one unmatched qualifier ("Berlin, Germany"/"Berlin").
  Renamed `PlaceIncomplete` — named for the incompleteness both share rather
  than a strength neither guarantees — with both readings documented. Not split:
  nothing needs to tell them apart, and inventing a distinction ahead of a
  consumer is what was refused for salary and employment type.

Mutation-checked 24 ways, all caught. Two survived the first pass and both were
real gaps, now closed: the clamp fix was tested on long POSTINGS but not long
PREFERENCES, and substituting a default for the handed-over posting facts was
invisible to the whole crate — the same untested-hand-off shape that bit the
command's tail expression earlier in this branch.

test(pipeline): pin what a killed resume run leaves on disk and what nothing cleans up (#1020)

* test(pipeline): pin what a killed resume run leaves on disk and what nothing cleans up

Tracing the recovery contract for a resume pipeline killed mid-run found that there is no recovery contract: `jobs::JobTracker::open`
sweeps interrupted jobs to `failed` on every startup and `AutopilotStore::mark_interrupted_runs` does the same for autopilot, but
`PipelineRunStore::open` runs migrations and a url normalisation and nothing else. A `pipeline_runs` row written `running` before the
first stage stays `running` forever after a kill.

These tests document that gap rather than assert it is correct.

`tests/pipeline_kill_recovery.rs` performs a real kill: the test binary re-executes itself as a child, the child opens the same stores
the app opens and writes the state a run interrupted during `draft` would have, and the parent kills the process outright before
reopening those files the way startup does. The run row and its partial stage trail come back untouched; the same kill's jobs.db row
comes back `failed` with a stated reason. That contrast is the finding, and the jobs.db half doubles as the positive control.

`a_crashed_running_run_locks_out_the_last_good_runs_report` pins the consequence against the real decision function: the orphan is
permanently the newest run for its posting, so `ensure_latest_run` refuses `regenerateSection` and `resolveFabrication` against the run
that actually holds the saved document, telling the user to wait for a run whose process no longer exists.

Mutation-checked four ways: neutering the jobs.db sweep, adding reconciliation to the run store, breaking the child readiness
handshake, and neutering `ensure_latest_run` each turn the relevant tests red.

fix(jobs): keep the scrape state alive across a route change (#1019)

* fix(jobs): keep the scrape state alive across a route change

The jobs scrape is a backend job that outlives the page, but everything
describing it lived in JobsPage/useScraping component state. Navigating to
Settings and back therefore threw away three things while the Rust job kept
running:

1. DATA LOSS. The last-search signature (and its replace latch) reset to '', so
   the next scrape compared the current criteria against nothing and latched
   replace:true, which clears the persisted postings cache the moment the first
   item streams. "Show more", whose entire contract is APPEND, destroyed the
   user's result set. The scrape FORM reset with it, so restoring only the
   signature would not have been enough: the criteria differed too, and the
   comparison would still have said "new search".
2. The in-flight jobId died, so the command bar showed neither progress nor
   Cancel while the always-mounted status bar still said a job was running, and
   the next search failed to supersede the orphan - two scrapes writing into one
   postings cache.
3. The per-board diagnostics (the "aggregator: 429 rate limited" strip, the only
   explanation of an empty result) were dropped, and dropped again when a scrape
   finished while the user was elsewhere.

All of it moves into JobsSlice, which already held listScrollTop for exactly
this reason. The store is memory-only (no persist middleware), so an app restart
clears it and there is no stale-job-across-restart case to design for.

`scraping` deliberately does NOT become a stored field that could desync from
the job id it describes: it stays local, seeded from the surviving id, and the
watchdog - which polls the job tracker, the authoritative terminal state -
reconciles it on remount. The watchdog now also recovers the per-board summaries
from the tracker's stored result, since the completion EVENT is emitted to
nobody while the page is unmounted.

The event handler reads identity synchronously through getState(), not a
subscribed value: it runs on backend events rather than React's schedule, so a
captured value would reintroduce exactly the staleness the old scrapeJobRef
existed to prevent.

The three sibling JobsPage tests now use the real session store instead of an
object stub, because the store is the seam under test.

* perf(jobs): subscribe to the session store per field, not wholesale

Moving the scrape state into the store is what made JobsPage read from it, so
the subscription shape is this branch's to own. Destructuring from an
unselected `useSessionStore()` subscribes to EVERY slice, so a background AI
generation, an autopilot run or a job-summary-cache write re-rendered a page
that carries the virtualized posting list plus several sort/filter memo passes.

One selector per field now, each returning a stored value rather than a fresh
object or array literal (which would defeat the default Object.is equality and
re-render anyway). The identity reads inside the `useJobEvents` handler stay
`getState()` on purpose - they run on backend events, not React's schedule.

JobsCommandBar and JobsSplitView had the same unselected read. Those predate
this branch, but they are children of the same page and JobsSplitView owns the
virtualized list, so leaving them would have made the fix nominal: an unrelated
slice write would still have re-rendered both. JobsSplitView's mount-time
`listScrollTop` capture becomes a `getState()` read, not a selector -
subscribing there would re-render the list on every scroll-save it makes.

Also from review:

* the jobs defaults become a factory (`makeJobsDefaults`). The slice holds
  arrays - `scrapeSummaries`, and `boards`/`companies` inside `scrapeForm` - and

fix(autopilot): jitter scheduled runs so default installs stop herding (#1018)

Track B3 of the architecture audit.

Schedules are clock-anchored, the tick is 60 s wide, and every record created
before the run-time picker defaults to 09:00. So every default-schedule install
in a time zone hits the same third-party APIs inside the same minute. This is
not theoretical here: the desktop log already shows scheduled runs failing with
`adzuna: HTTP 503`.

The offset is DETERMINISTIC per autopilot, derived from its id, not random —
that is the whole design. A random delay would have meant sleeping inside the
tick, which breaks the two properties everything else is built on: catch-up
after a missed occurrence, and no-double-run once `lastRunAt` is stamped at or
after the occurrence. Shifting the OCCURRENCE instead keeps it a single
well-defined instant, so both still hold, and tests stay reproducible.

FNV-1a rather than `DefaultHasher`: the standard hasher is explicitly not stable
across Rust releases, and an offset that moved on a toolchain bump would
silently shift every user's schedule. Ids are UUIDs, so the low bits are already
well distributed.

Ten minutes: wide enough to spread a herd across ten tick windows, far enough
under the shortest interval (hourly) that a shifted occurrence can never
overtake the next one, small enough not to surprise someone who picked 09:00.
That upper bound is a `const _: () = assert!(...)` beside the constant rather
than a test — a test comparing two constants is a tautology clippy rejects, and
this makes a bad value unbuildable instead of merely reported.

Tests cover the offset being stable for an id and inside the window, the
occurrence moving by exactly the offset, and the behaviour a user would notice:
between the nominal time and the offset, today's occurrence has NOT been reached,
so the latest is still yesterday's. Plus a full-day minute-by-minute sweep
asserting exactly one transition — one run per day, no double-run, no skip.

Mutation-checked: making the offset always zero fails
`jitter_actually_spreads_a_herd` with "200 autopilots landed in only 1 distinct
minutes".

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

test(extension): pin the mv3 permission surface against the readme's promises (#1017)

Track D2 of the architecture audit, and the last open piece of Track D.

`manifest.ts` is the source of truth for claims this project makes OUTSIDE the
repo: to Chrome Web Store and AMO reviewers, in the extension README's
"Permissions — minimal & justified" table, and on the landing privacy page.
Nothing asserted any of it. Widening a permission is a two-line edit, and the
widened build would reach store review — and the user — with the old
justification still printed beside it. Store review is the wrong place to find
out: a rejection costs a release cycle, and an ACCEPTED over-broad permission
costs the claim.

Pinned:

* the permission list, written out BY HAND. A test that loops over the thing it
  guards catches additions only — delete an entry and the assertion deletes
  itself;
* a DENYLIST of permissions the extension must never hold, which is the half
  that survives a careless update. Mutation-checked: adding `tabs` to the
  manifest AND to the allowed literal still fails here;
* host permissions checked as a PROPERTY — every entry must parse to loopback —
  not by string equality, so `http://127.0.0.1.evil.com/*` cannot pass by merely
  looking right. Mutation-checked;
* both targets compared to each other, so a per-target delta cannot smuggle a
  permission into one build;
* MV3, no CSP loosening, no static `content_scripts` (Scan mode injects on a
  click, bounded by `activeTab`; a static block would run unbidden on every
  matching page — a different product);
* Firefox's `data_collection_permissions: ['none']`, the assertion to AMO that
  nothing leaves the device. If that ever stops being true, this failing is the
  intended prompt to declare the real categories rather than ship a false one.

Plus README parity in both directions, because the table is the justification a
reviewer actually reads: a requested permission missing from it is an
undocumented capability, and deleting the "we do not request `<all_urls>`,
`tabs`, `webRequest`" paragraph now fails too — otherwise the denylist would
still be enforced while corresponding to nothing published.

Test files are excluded from the extension tsconfig and
`rewrite-preset-parity.test.ts` already reads with `node:fs`, so the README check
needs no new tooling.

fix(scripts): stop a doc comment from promoting a hook to a subscriber (#1016)

The AI review flagged `MonitoringPage` as declared-but-not-subscribing. It was
right, and the cause is worse than a stale entry: discovery matched identifiers
against raw source, so PROSE that names a hook counted as a call to it.

A declaration slice runs to the next `export`, which means the doc comment
belonging to the hook BELOW lands inside the preceding hook's body. `use-jobs.ts`
documents `useJob` with "a `useJobEvents()` subscription MUST be mounted
somewhere in the tree" — so the plain `useQuery` hook above it, `useJobQueue`,
was promoted to a subscription hook by a sentence, and every file calling that
query was dragged into the inventory. That is the same structural fact this repo
already recorded from the other direction: a doc comment sits above its item, so
anything anchored on the item before swallows it.

Discovery now blanks comments and string/template literals before matching. A
hook name inside a string is a mention, not a call, and a commented-out
subscription is not one either. It is a scanner rather than a regex on purpose:
`//.*$` would eat the rest of a line after a URL in a string literal, silently
DROPPING a real call — the one failure direction a guard must not have.
Characters are replaced one-for-one with spaces so match offsets stay valid.

Result: `useJobQueue` correctly drops out (15 hooks, not 16), and with it the
`MonitoringPage` entry, which is removed. The other four wrappers were verified
by hand and are genuine — `useWorkerActivity` and `useAutoIndex` call
`useJobEvents`, `useMenuIntents` registers `api.menu.onNavigate`/`onAction`, and
`useUpdater` subscribes directly.

Tests: 35, up from 29. New cases pin the shipped bug (the next hook's doc
comment), a commented-out call, a listener that appears only inside a string, and
that stripping preserves length and line structure.

test(renderer): make surviving navigation a build-time question, not an audit (#1015)

* test(renderer): make surviving navigation a build-time question, not an audit

The autopilot bug was one instance of a class: a subscription only receives
events while its component is mounted, but the Rust work it describes does not
unmount. Leave the route and the events emitted while away — including the
terminal one — are dropped, the component's progress state is discarded, and the
UI renders idle for work that is still running.

An audit found the same shape across the jobs scrape, the résumé pipeline, the
Ollama model pull, the embeddings re-index and more. Auditing again after every
new feature is not a plan, so this asks the question at the moment the code is
written instead.

`check-event-subscriptions.mjs` discovers the subscription-hook family from
`services/` by the one idiom they all share (`api.<ns>.on<Event>(`) — discovered,
not hardcoded, so a NEW subscription hook is covered the day it is written — then
requires every file outside `services/` that calls one to be declared with its
mount lifetime. `always` needs no argument; `route-scoped` needs a note saying
what is dropped and why that is acceptable. Both directions are checked, so the
list cannot rot.

It earned its keep immediately: it found three subscribers a 34-agent audit of
the same question had missed, all three reaching `useUpdater` — which turns out
to have three independent instances, each with its own subscription and its own
local status.

The `route-scoped` entries are a DEBT LIST, not approvals. Each records what that
file loses today, including the largest instance: `use-resume-pipeline-session`
mounts FOUR subscriptions and is called from `TailorFlow/GeneratingPanel`, which
is route-scoped AND conditionally rendered, so a résumé generation loses its
stage events and its streamed draft. Exactly one entry is an accepted non-defect
(the monitoring activity feed has no per-run state to preserve), and it says so.

Mutation-checked in both directions: a new feature file that subscribes fails by
name, and breaking the discovery regex trips the vacuity guards rather than
silently passing everything — the failure mode that would make this theatre. The
16 unit tests cover the same, plus three that run against the REAL renderer, so
discovery drifting off the actual source cannot stay green.

Lives in `scripts/` beside the other drift guards rather than in a vitest file:
the renderer tsconfig carries no node types, and the `lint-format` CI job has no
path filter, so a diff that misses the renderer cannot skip it.

Deliberately NOT shipped: a companion "state machines must be re-armable" guard.
The autopilot machine's real defect was dropping an UNSOLICITED backend event in
a terminal state, and every predicate I could write for that was either vacuous
(all three machines already reach a busy state via RESET) or arbitrary.

* fix(scripts): close two ways a subscription could walk past the guard

Both review findings were right, and both mattered more than they looked: a
guard that can be stepped around is worse than no guard, because it reports
green.

CodeRabbit — discovery matched the EXPORTED hook name, so

declaring its own same-named local function is no longer reported as a

fix(autopilot): keep a run in flight visible after navigating away (#1013)

* fix(autopilot): keep a run in flight visible after navigating away

Reported: created an autopilot, ran it, went to Settings, came back to a card
that looked finished — but the status bar still said a job was running, and
clicking Run answered "a run is already in progress for this autopilot".

Every one of those three signals was correct except the card. The backend held
the run for its full duration (the log shows 301s, dominated by the 300s
semantic re-rank ceiling), the RunGuard refused the second click on purpose,
and the status bar reads the global job registry. Only the card lied, because
its run state is component-local:

* `useAutopilotRun` keeps `runStates`/`stepLogs` in a `useReducer` inside
  `AutopilotPage`, so a route change discards them and the card re-renders
  'idle' — and `inProgress` is deliberately not badged, so nothing else on the
  card contradicts that;
* the same hook owns the step-event subscription, so every step emitted while
  the user was away, terminal `complete` included, was dropped;
* `runAutopilot`'s `onSuccess` invalidation belongs to the unmounted observer,
  so the finished run's found jobs never reached the list either.

Fixes, all reading truth that already existed:

* fall back to the persisted `runStatus === 'inProgress'` when this mount has
  no local state for an autopilot, so the card shows 'scraping' and the Run
  button stays disabled;
* let the machine's `idle` accept the mid-run vocabulary, not just the start —
  a card that rejoins mid-run gets `scrape_done`/`complete` with no preceding
  `scrape_start`, and dropping those pinned it back to idle;
* let the terminal states re-arm on `scrape_start`, so the scheduler's next
  occurrence doesn't stream underneath a card frozen on the last outcome;
* invalidate the list when a run ends, which also fixes scheduled runs never
  showing their results until the next navigation;
* stop reverting to 'idle' on `already-running`. That refusal is proof a run is
  in flight, so idle re-armed the button for a click the backend refuses again.

Mutation-checked: reverting the `runStatus` fallback fails exactly one test.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(autopilot): stop a refused run from stranding the card in a busy state

Review found a real hole in the first commit. Holding the optimistic 'scraping'
after an `already-running` refusal assumed the concurrent run would announce its
end — but the Rust failure arm calls `job_fail` and returns early WITHOUT
emitting any step, so on a failed run no terminal event ever arrives and the
card sits on 'scraping' forever, Run permanently disabled.

Rather than bound it with a timeout, give the two authorities an explicit order:

* this mount's machine wins once it has actually OBSERVED the run — any state
  other than 'idle' came from a step event or the click itself, and it knows the
  finer phase;
* the persisted `runStatus` decides otherwise.

So `already-running` goes back to 'idle', which is now the value that hands the
card to the backend: it still displays as running for as long as `runStatus`
says `inProgress`, and it clears the moment that resolves — including to
`failed`, the case with no event at all.

The order is load-bearing in both directions, and both are pinned: reading the
backend first flickers a locally-'done' card back to 'scraping' until the
invalidation lands, and reading only the local state is the original bug.
Mutation-checked — swapping to backend-first fails
`keeps_a_locally_observed_terminal_state_while_the_list_query_is_still_stale`.

Also adds the `cancelled` invalidation case CodeRabbit asked for: it is the other
terminal step, and `finish_cancelled` clears the live status and wipes the prior
run's summaries, so a card left on pre-cancel data shows an abandoned run.

test(export): enforce adr-002's golden-parity claim for the first time (#1012)

ADR-002 says the PDF and DOCX backends are kept "in golden parity where the
design requires, pinned by deterministic golden snapshot tests". The
per-backend tests were real, but nothing rendered ONE document through BOTH and
checked the same facts came out. The parity half of the claim was documented,
not enforced — the gap the architecture audit filed as Track A3.

Not hypothetical for this codebase: DOCX body bold had never rendered at all,
and a macOS incident shipped with the two formats disagreeing. An ATS reads the
extracted text, so a fact that survives one export and not the other means the
candidate submits a materially different résumé depending on which button they
pressed — and only the backend that still had the content would look fine in
its own snapshot.

The harness renders every canonical template through both backends from the
same `ExportRequest`, extracts text from each, and asserts a fixed set of
facts (name, section headings, employer, title, a bullet, degree) survived
into both.

**Anchored on the SOURCE, not on the other backend.** Comparing PDF text to
DOCX text is the shape this repo has shipped broken repeatedly — two derived
values with nothing absolute behind them, so a change that drops Education from
BOTH stays green forever. Each rendering is checked against the input fixture
instead, which cannot pass that way.

It asserts facts rather than the fixture verbatim, because line breaks,
hyphenation, column order and glyph runs legitimately differ between a Typst
page and a Word document. What may not differ is whether a fact survived.

Includes a vacuity guard: an extractor returning almost nothing would make
every containment check pass trivially, so both extractions must exceed a
length floor before they are trusted.

Runs the whole roster rather than a sample, for the reason the sibling PDF
matrix gives — a template nobody rendered is a template nobody validated.

Mutations, both red at baseline-green: making the DOCX renderer silently skip
the Education section, and making the DOCX extractor return an empty string
(caught by the vacuity guard, not by the parity assertions).

fix(evidence): stop filing academic records as work experience (#1011)

* fix(evidence): stop filing german academic records as work experience

Found by sweeping every term in the renderer's `SECTION_LEXICON` through
`classify_section` — 197 terms, which nothing had ever compared. The two sides
answer the same question from different data: the TS lexicon drives
`detectSections`, this classifier drives `extract_evidence`.

**The bug.** German "Akademischer Werdegang" — a standard heading for an
academic record — contains `werdegang`, which is an unconditional entry in
`EXPERIENCE_HEADINGS`, and that test runs first. So it classified as
Experience. Not a cosmetic mislabel: prose under an Experience heading reaches
`extract_evidence`'s role arm, so degree entries became work bullets under
roles the candidate never held. Same failure the module already documents for
"Kenntnisse und Erfahrungen", one list away.

Fixed with a closed list of three exact phrases checked BEFORE the experience
test, not by generalising. The general fix — letting
`AMBIGUOUS_EXPERIENCE_HEADINGS` yield to education as it yields to summary and
skills — would overturn a documented decision: Education and Projects are
excluded from that yield set on purpose, because "Project Experience" really is
a work history in a consultant's CV. These three phrases have no second
reading, so they need no rule. A control asserts "Beruflicher Werdegang" and
bare "Werdegang" are still Experience, so the exception did not swallow the
rule.

**The wider gap.** The same sweep found 44 lexicon terms classifying as `Other`
— coverage gaps rather than misfiles, since the section checks just don't run.
Closed the ones for the two markets the owner prioritised and that carry no
ambiguity: `praxiserfahrung`, `studium` (de), `istruzione`, `esperienze` (it).
`istruzione` is the very heading `resume_conventions("it")` teaches the model
to write, so the producer and the recogniser disagreed about Italian education.

The remaining 40 are enumerated in `KNOWN_MISSES` rather than tolerated in
bulk. The list is asserted in BOTH directions: a new lexicon term that nothing
recognises fails, and fixing one without removing it from the list fails too —
so it can only shrink deliberately. That turns a silent gap into a reviewed
inventory. They are mostly Summary/Skills synonyms in fr/es/it/nl/pt, and they
are not free to close: these consts are substring tests, and `expertise`,
`portfolio` and `studi` have second readings (Italian "studio" contains
`studi`), so they need word-bounded handling rather than a bare push.

`Languages` terms landing on `Skills` are allowlisted explicitly with the
reason — `SectionKind` has no `Languages` variant, and "Sprachkenntnisse" was
rejected as a German producer heading for exactly this — rather than being
swept up by the wrong-bucket rule.

The fixture is a flattened copy of `SECTION_LEXICON` because Rust cannot parse
the TS source; a vitest guard asserts the copy still equals the live lexicon,
which is what stops the Rust sweep from checking yesterday's vocabulary and
reporting green.

Four mutations run, all red at baseline-green: dropping the precedence branch,
removing a newly-taught term, shrinking KNOWN_MISSES without fixing anything,
and fixing a miss while leaving it listed.

ci: enforce the Rust toolchain pin instead of asking for it in a comment (#1010)

* ci: enforce the rust toolchain pin instead of asking for it in a comment

The pin itself already shipped and is correct: `rust-toolchain.toml` pins
1.97.1, and both `dtolnay/rust-toolchain` uses are pinned to the SHA for that
same version. What was missing is any enforcement.

The two halves cannot reference each other — that action does not read toolchain
files, its `@rev` IS the version selector — so the only thing tying them
together was a comment in three files saying "bump both together". That is the
shape this repo treats as a defect: a stated invariant with nothing checking it.

The failure is quiet, which is what makes it worth a check. Bump the TOML alone
and CI keeps building on the old compiler; bump the action alone and every
developer's machine drifts off what CI validates. Neither goes red on its own —
the pin simply stops meaning anything, which is exactly the state it was created
to end.

`scripts/check-toolchain-pin.mjs` asserts four things: the channel is an exact
three-part version rather than a floating one; every `dtolnay/rust-toolchain`
use under `.github/` carries a trailing `# <version>` comment (an opaque SHA is
unreviewable by construction, so the comment is load-bearing, not decoration);
every one of those declared versions equals the channel; and the Cargo MSRV is
not above the pin, since that pairing cannot compile at all.

It deliberately does NOT verify that the SHA truly is that version — that needs
a network call, and it is not the mistake people make. The realistic error is
updating one place and forgetting the other, which is fully catchable offline.

Wired into the `lint-format` job, which has no path filter and so runs on every
PR — a toolchain drift guard that only fires when Rust files change would miss
the case where someone edits only the workflow. The three comments now name
their enforcer instead of asking nicely.

Guard is mutation-tested five ways against the real repo (bump either half
alone, float the channel back to `stable`, strip a version comment, raise the
MSRV past the pin) — all red, tree restored clean — plus 11 black-box CLI tests
over a fake repo tree, following `check-tech-radar.test.mjs`. One of those
covers removing CI's pin entirely, which would otherwise pass vacuously: with
nothing to compare, nothing disagrees.

feat(scraping): add freehire as the aggregator's keyless tier (#1008)

* feat(scraping): add freehire as the aggregator's keyless tier

Issue #1002, opened by freehire's maintainer, who disclosed the interest. We
publicly committed to shipping it in the next release.

Implemented from their published openapi.yaml rather than from the PR they
offered. The reason is rights, not code quality: this repo has no CLA, so a
contribution stays under its author's copyright and cannot be relicensed, and
ADR-023 names commercial licensing as a rationale. Reading their PR and
rewriting it would be derivative — the worst of both worlds — so the spec is
the only source used.

What it buys: every other provider needs an API key, so a fresh install gets a
needs-keys skip and zero jobs. freehire answers unauthenticated, so the
aggregator board can return results before the user has configured anything.
It is not a better source than the keyed tiers and is never preferred over
one — it runs LAST, after Adzuna, JSearch and Jooble have each failed to
produce a decisive result, and only a non-empty answer from it short-circuits.
An empty answer from a provider nobody chose is not evidence about the search,
so it must not swallow a configured provider's failure diagnostic.

Two consequences worth calling out rather than burying:

`needs_keys()` is now always false, because a keyless tier is always
"configured". That is the point — the skip existed because a keyless search
could only ever return nothing. The cost, accepted and tested: a keyless user
whose freehire search finds nothing reads "no jobs found" rather than a prompt
to add keys. A keyring READ FAULT is still classified separately, so the one
case the old `false` protected is unaffected.

Failures degrade to Ok(empty), never Err — the only provider with that rule.
Every other one reports its failure because a stored key means the user asked
for it specifically. Nobody opted into this one, so surfacing its outage would
turn a third party's downtime into an error banner on a search the user never
aimed at them. There is no SLA and no rate-limit header of any kind (verified:
no X-RateLimit-*, no Retry-After), so it is treated as always-possibly-absent.

Uses the documented /agent/jobs/search with `q` and
`description_format=markdown` — NOT the undocumented /jobs/search taking
`query`, which is what the issue described and what a first pass reached for;
building from the published spec is the whole basis for implementing this
ourselves. Markdown up front is also what keeps scoring from needing a
per-result detail fetch.

A guessed country is deliberately not sent as a filter: the aggregator defaults
`country` to "de" when the caller supplied none, and pinning a keyless tier to
that guess would reproduce the guessed-market bug already fixed for Adzuna.
`location` is unused because the documented search has no city parameter at
all, and folding a city into the full-text `q` would drop every posting that
does not spell its city out, remote ones included.

Egress: freehire.me is in the inventory with a public_name, which made the
landing drift guard fail until the privacy page, README and SECURITY named it.
That guard shipped two PRs ago for exactly this, and this is the first new
egress since — it worked.

Every behaviour above is pinned by a test that was mutation-checked: green at
baseline, red with the feature deleted, restored. The one claim that did not
survive checking is recorded in the test rather than quietly dropped — the
ordering guard catches "moved ahead of the keyed tiers" but would NOT catch
"moved one rung up past Jooble", because the fixture short-circuits at Adzuna.

things.

supplied, a real location: two London-relevant Adzuna hits were discarded for
up to fifty globally-unfiltered freehire ones. That is the guessed-market bug
this repo already fixed for Adzuna, re-entered through a new door. It now
merges, sparse hits first so dedupe's first-seen-wins order preserves them.

The comment justifying the original behaviour claimed "the free-text location
still reaches `q`, so a real place name is not lost". That was false, and I
made it false myself: the sentence was written before I removed `location`
from the function on discovering the API has no city parameter at all. On a
guessed market this tier is location-blind, which is precisely why it must not
replace hits that are not.

**It swallowed every configured provider's failure diagnostic.** Reproduced:
three revoked keys, and `BoardScrapeSummary.error` came back `None`. Since
`needs_keys()` is now permanently false, no surface anywhere in the app would
have told the user their key was broken — indefinitely. It is now skipped
whenever a configured provider actually failed.

guessed-market branch records its fall-through in `adzuna_configured_failed`,

- The privacy page said freehire runs after every keyed tier "has come back
  empty or failed". A keyed tier's `Ok(empty)` is decisive and returns

  checks that a named host appears, not that the claim around it is true.
- `freehire_slugless_rows_key_off_their_url_not_each_other` asserted only
  pairwise inequality and stayed GREEN when the reviewer mutated the fallback
  id to a non-deterministic counter — a change that would break cross-run
  dedupe and resurface every slugless posting as new on each re-scrape. It now
  asserts the concrete value. This is the repo's recorded pass-for-the-wrong-
  reason shape and I reproduced it in my own new test.
- `description` now goes through `html_to_markdown` like every sibling
  provider. The "already markdown, no conversion needed" rationale was wrong
  in both directions: the call is free (it early-returns tag-free input
  verbatim) and it is the only defence when freehire's upstreams leave HTML in
  a field labelled markdown.

  still described a three-provider chain and claimed "none configured →
  keyless-empty"; `Scraper::needs_keys` and the `boards.ts` skip contract still

refactor(platform): own the test data-dir override where the rule says it belongs (#1006)

The Stop gate flagged std::env::var in the new SSRF test. The architecture test
disagreed and passed, because R4 exempts files it classifies as tests - so the
rule was enforceable everywhere except the one place a test would actually reach
for the variable. The gate was right in spirit: platform/config.rs's own module
doc calls it the sole owner of that env var and says no other module may read
it.

Rather than argue the exemption, the override moved to where the rule points.
platform::config::DataDirGuard is a test-only RAII scope: a caller names a
directory, never the variable. It restores on Drop instead of at the end of the
test body, so a panicking assertion cannot leak the override into whatever runs
next - which the previous inline version could.

Also added #[serial] to data_dir_honors_env_then_falls_back. It mutates the same
process-global variable directly and had no serialization, so it could race the
new test. That gap was pre-existing but only became reachable once a second test
started scoping the same variable.

The test file now contains no env access and does not name the variable in
prose either, so both the gate's ast-grep matcher and R4's literal search are
satisfied for the right reason rather than by an exemption.

fix(pipeline): catch per-section language drift, drop empty sections, and keep the regenerate language (#1003)

* fix(pipeline): catch per-section language drift, drop empty sections, keep the regenerate language

Three owner-reported defects, all downstream of one architectural change: PRs
#969 and #992 moved generation from ONE whole-document call to per-section
calls that cannot see their siblings. Before that, coherence was free.

Language drift. content.language_mismatch read the whole document, and
languages_align returns the DOMINANT language, so a majority vote hid exactly
the reported case. Measured: one Italian section in a long English resume went
undetected, two undetected, three detected. A per-section pass now runs when
the document-level read comes back clean.

It is scoped POSITIVELY to Summary/Experience/Projects rather than by excluding
Skills. Review caught why that matters: SectionKind has six variants and
classify_section has no heading list for Certifications, Awards, Publications
or Languages-spoken, so all of them land in Other. A correct English "AWS
Certified Solutions Architect (Professional, 2022)" block clears the character
floor and reads as non-English - an exclusion list silently admits every kind
nobody thought of. A false Critical here blanks keywordCoverage and suppresses
every alignment finding on the whole document, so the cost of over-reach is
higher than the miss.

Empty sections. My own #998 regression: "order the sections EXACTLY as … do
not drop" read as a manifest plus a ban on omitting anything, so the model
emitted Projects and Publications with nothing in them. The prompt now frames
the list as an order, not a checklist.

The guard is a Warning, not a Critical, and the severity is the design. repair
acts on Criticals and its remedy is to REGENERATE the section - asked to fill
an empty PROJECTS the model would invent projects, a fabrication in the one
part of this pipeline built to prevent them. Removal is the right remedy and
model::adapter::push_nonempty_section already does it structurally, so nothing
empty reaches the rendered document.

Regenerate language. useTailorPipeline re-detected from jobDesc every render
and treated "I could not tell" as "it is English", discarding a language the
run already knew. It now prefers the persisted value - normalized through
toLanguageCode first, because extractMetadata persists a display NAME
("German") while every other writer stores an ISO code and save_application
merges both into one record. Passing "German" through would have been worse
than the bug: normalize_language truncates it to "ge", which matches no
languages_align arm, turning the language checks off entirely for that
document.

An audit measured what #969/#992 broke when generation moved from one
whole-document call to per-section calls that cannot see their siblings. Five
findings, one root cause each side of the same seam: the splice trusted the
model's reply, and the accept rule could not see the damage.

A repair round could silently delete a job. company_survives lowercased the
ENTIRE generated document and substring-searched for the employer, so a
Summary reading "…at Acme Payments and Globex Logistics" spared the deletion

factual.dropped_role never fired, round accepted and persisted. Survival is now
tested against the generated EXPERIENCE section, all of its lines, so an
ordinary bullet reword still matches.

section. is_usable_replacement checked for a fence tag, a leading heading and
one body line, and nothing about how many sections came back. Measured: 6
sections to 10, and because reorder_sections is a stable sort, linearize merely
parked the duplicates adjacent - the exported PDF showed four sections twice.
Under mutation it compounded to 4x as the loop re-accepted round after round.

A reply for a DIFFERENT section was accepted. The target was resolved by
SectionKey and the reply spliced without re-classifying it, so asking for
SUMMARY and receiving SKILLS silently destroyed the summary and created a
second skills section, which the next round then could not find. The reply's
own heading is now re-classified and a mismatch is discarded - the right remedy
for a bad attempt is to drop it, not to raise a Critical that would ask the
model to regenerate again.

invented link in a second Projects section produced zero Criticals. The
Critical-severity consumer now reads every matching section; the two
Warning-severity consumers keep the cheaper lookup, since the residual risk
there costs a missed Warning rather than a missed Critical.

round_is_worse could only see Criticals and absences, while its sibling
humanize_is_worse also guarded coverage and voice - and repair runs FIRST,
makes up to eight blind per-section rewrites, and had the weaker rule. It now
reverts on a drop in roles_output, the one metric that saw the deleted job, and
shares humanize's coverage guard rather than duplicating it.

* feat(pipeline): let a section rewrite see the document it belongs to

Before #969/#992 a resume was generated by ONE model call, so language, voice
and tense coherence came free. The staged pipeline broke generation into
per-section calls that cannot see their siblings and replaced that implicit
guarantee with a prompt instruction - and instructions drift. Three
user-visible bugs followed, including a resume whose summary was English, work
experience Italian, and skills English again.

repair_user passed the source resume, the one section being rewritten, its
issues and an optional note. Nothing told the model what the rest of the
document looked like. It now also receives a compact anchor: the Summary,
which carries the register, and one representative Experience bullet, which
carries tense and voice - each excluded by SectionKind when it IS the section
being rewritten, so a rewrite never matches the text it is replacing.

An anchor rather than the whole document because this is charged up to
MAX_SECTIONS_PER_ROUND x max_repair_attempts = 8 times per run. Capped at
SIBLING_CONTEXT_CAP, roughly twice the measured worst case in this crate's own
fixtures and far below the whole-document cap humanize uses for its single
pass. The trade: drift confined to Skills or Education against the anchor is
not prevented, only detected.

This is model-generated text re-entering a prompt, so ADR-010 applies exactly
as it does to a scraped job ad. document_context is registered in
FENCE_TAG_PATTERNS and covered by the existing load-bearing forgery loop;
removing the registration lets a forged closing tag leak through, which the
test now proves.

The user's own regenerate-this-section button inherits all of it, since
resume_pipeline_regenerate_section calls the same function.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* feat(pipeline): revert a repair round that introduces cross-section incoherence

An audit found the codebase's only two cross-section coherence checks -
duplicate.bullet and consistency.skill_not_demonstrated - are computed and then
thrown away. repair acts on Criticals only, humanize on voice.* only. Measured
consequences, both accepted and persisted: a round that doubled the whole
document produced 5 duplicate.bullet warnings at duplicateRatio 1.00 and
shipped; a round that deleted an employment entry produced 4
skill_not_demonstrated warnings and shipped.

The naive fix is to revert when those warnings are present, and it is wrong.
The same audit measured them false-positiving under per-section generation:
rewording two Experience bullets to drop the exact tokens - the ordinary
outcome of a rewrite that cannot see the Skills section - raises four warnings
on a truthful document. An absolute threshold would revert good rounds and
would need calibrating against noise.

So the term is a DELTA, not a count. The question is not whether the document
carries cross-section warnings but whether THIS ROUND introduced any that were
not there before. Four before and four after reverts nothing; four before and
nine after reverts. That needs no threshold, is immune to the measured baseline
false positives, and matches the before/after shape round_is_worse already uses
for its newly-introduced-absence term.

Per code rather than summed, so a round that fixes two duplicate.bullet
warnings while introducing two skill_not_demonstrated ones cannot hide a
regression behind an unrelated improvement - a case a summed total reads as
flat, and which the mutation check confirmed only the per-code form catches.

Also closes two advisories from the security review of da4926f0: the anchor is
trimmed once at its source, so repair_system's gate and repair_user's own
emptiness test can no longer disagree about whether a document_context block
exists; and the context rule now says to match the language and tense OBSERVED
there, naming it a writing sample rather than asking the model to conform to
untrusted content.
